items.title: Surveillance and 'constant paranoia': Western diplomats tell BBC of life in war-time Moscow
items.summary: Officials compare working in Russia since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine to the Cold War era.
items.content:
Image caption, Ex-US and French ambassadors Lynne Tracy and Pierre LÃ©vy were among those to speak to the BBC of their time in Moscow
"Being the ambassador to Russia was probably the hardest assignment of my career," Lynne Tracy, who represented the US in Moscow from 2023 to 2025, tells the BBC.
US, UK and European diplomats once played a crucial role in Russia, defusing tensions even at the worst moments of the Cold War.
But now, deemed "unfriendly" by President Vladimir Putin's government, Western ambassadors are under constant surveillance, isolated and increasingly cut off from the country they were sent to understand, as the war in Ukraine grinds on through its fifth year.
The BBC has spoken to five diplomats who have served in Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion.
They compare current pressure levels to the Cold War era - when Western embassies were monitored through physical surveillance, listening devices hidden inside gifts , and "spy dust" - a near invisible chemical agent used to track officials.
Hundreds of Russian diplomats were expelled from countries in Europe and the US after the war began in 2022. Moscow responded in kind, declaring hundreds of Western diplomats persona non grata and leaving many embassies short-staffed.
Tracy's 30-year career took her to countries like Pakistan, where she survived an armed attack in 2008. But she says that even under constant physical threat, her posting in Peshawar was, in a sense, easier than Russia.
"There, I still felt that there were things within my control. What made Moscow more difficult were the high levels of uncertainty."
The constant pressure from Russian counterintelligence was the primary source of such uncertainty, she recalls.
Image caption, Tracy pictured leaving Russia's Foreign Ministry after being summoned by Moscow in 2023
Russian diplomats in the West also complain of such unfair treatment. But according to the diplomats who spoke to the BBC, the scope and tactics of Moscow's intelligence services are far greater.
"Expect listening devices, expect cameras in every single room of your house," a former European diplomat says of the warning he received before leaving for Moscow.
Another ex-ambassador says they were forced to dismiss two Russian employees after Moscow's domestic security service, the FSB, tried to recruit them, demanding that they report on everything going on at the diplomatic mission.
The pair told the embassy instead, who let them go - "otherwise, they could have faced some sort of criminal prosecution".
Meanwhile, Russians who would ordinarily build relationships with diplomatic staff - such as those working in academia and culture - are also being intimidated into avoiding contact with Western officials.
One former ambassador says his guests were once "tailed" by FSB agents right up to the doors of the embassy.
Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage - and Russia is the chief suspect
Just this June, guests invited to the British ambassador's residence in Moscow for the King's birthday celebrations said they had been harassed by pro-Kremlin activists and state-media journalists, and then questioned by the police.
One of the guests says he has since declined several invitations to events at Western embassies out of fear.
One former ambassador says "constant paranoia" has driven a number of officials to quit their jobs. Even after leaving Russia himself, he adds, he was looking over his shoulder for months.
'Generals prove what they can do in war. The same is true for diplomats'
In the immediate aftermath of the invasion, there were discussions across Europe about whether to recall ambassadors or stop working in Russia altogether, says former French ambassador Pierre LÃ©vy.
He remembers calling Paris immediately to say pulling their envoys would be a mistake, feeling that the worse relations became, the more important they would be.
The invasion quickly transformed their work, says another ex-European ambassador; the co-operation required for their usual efforts on bilateral relations, trade and joint projects was now impossible.
And for those who stayed in Russia, the war left them with a host of new priorities beyond supporting their own citizens and companies.
Firstly, countries viewed as unfriendly by Moscow still wanted at least some channel of communication with Russian officials to get an accurate picture of what was happening inside the country.
But they also had to protect their staff and keep their embassies functioning.
Image caption, Pierre LÃ©vy (second from the left) and Lynne Tracy (second from the right) pictured at the funeral service for opposition leader Alexei Navalny in March 2024
After Russia's ban on hiring foreign nationals in 2021, the US embassy's facilities team was left significantly understaffed. Ðven a minor plumbing issue like a leaking pipe could turn into a major problem, draining the time of diplomatic workers.
One diplomat recalls discussing staffing shortages with a Russian official, who advised him not to get too upset. "He said, 'at least you still have the chef'."
Financial sanctions imposed by Western governments to support Ukraine created different day-to-day difficulties. After Russian banks were cut off from the Swift payment network, and Mastercard and Visa suspended operations in Russia, many embassies struggled with basic operating expenses.
A former ambassador recalls simply running out of cash and being unable to pay his staff - until another diplomat, who was selling his car after being expelled, brought the rubles to the embassy in a suitcase.
"It's completely insane," the diplomat laughs. "But you had to look at it with a sense of humour."
Image caption, A wooden replica of the Great Seal of the US was given to the American ambassador to Russia as a gift in 1945 - it was later found to contain a listening device
Russian officials make little secret of their attitude towards Western diplomats. They have openly accused those from "unfriendly countries" of engaging in "espionage".
Moscow has been particularly critical of those who show an interest in expressions of dissent against the Kremlin and, according to Russian journalist Alexei Venediktov, has effectively banned most Russian officials from speaking to Western embassies.
This has only worsened relations with the West, says Venediktov, who recalls telling Russian officials: "You are being misunderstood precisely because of your own actions - because ambassadors cannot do their jobs."
Today, Moscow has little to no contact with many Western governments, says one ex-European ambassador. "There are no calls, no meetings at ministerial level."
But they say this has made diplomats all the more important, left with the responsibility to communicate their governments' positions to Moscow.
"Generals prove what they can do during a war. The same is true for diplomats. When things get really difficult, every single thing you do actually matters."
Lynne Tracy left Moscow in 2025 feeling she had accomplished her primary mission: the US Embassy had held firm.
But she is also proud of the work she and her team did to maintain connection between Americans and ordinary Russians.
"Because at some point, government-to-government relations will have a chance to improve - and those ties between people will be there to help speed the improvement."

items.title: US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran - The Guardian
items.summary: US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran  The Guardian
items.content:
Faisal bin Farhan of Saudi Arabia, Ishaq Dar of Pakistan, Hakan Fidan of Turkey, Jean-Noël Barrot of France, Johann Wadephul of Germany, Ed Miliband of the UK and Antonio Tajani of Italy at the summit in Istanbul on Friday. Photograph: Massimo Percossi/EPA
Faisal bin Farhan of Saudi Arabia, Ishaq Dar of Pakistan, Hakan Fidan of Turkey, Jean-Noël Barrot of France, Johann Wadephul of Germany, Ed Miliband of the UK and Antonio Tajani of Italy at the summit in Istanbul on Friday. Photograph: Massimo Percossi/EPA
US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran
Multinational ‘anti-war bloc’ uses Istanbul summit to call for a diplomatic solution to Middle East crisis
Foreign ministers at a summit of eight European and Middle Eastern countries have urged the US and Israel not to renews their attacks on Iran, warning a fresh outbreak of fighting would spread conflict and push oil prices even higher.
The development of a new multinational “anti-war bloc” represents a challenge to the increasingly open plans by the US and Israel to relaunch strikes on Iran while talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme remain deadlocked.
The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, joint convener of the summit in Istanbul, said: “Military intervention in Iran is not any kind of solution. We agreed that a new military attack would spread the war and the conflict in the region. All the countries around the table do not want the war to spread even more, once again.”
Ministers also demanded an end to the Houthi assaults on Saudi Arabia, and an immediate opening of the strait of Hormuz currently blockaded by Iranian ships and drones.
Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, said another war between Iran and the US would be bad for both sides, and only worsen rising oil prices, which have hit their highest level since May. Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, also urged both sides to embrace diplomacy.
The Istanbul meeting, an unprecedented gathering of regional and European leaders initiated by Turkey and Germany , represented a rare chance for European ministers to have any input into the crises afflicting the Middle East, including in Yemen, Palestine and Iran. They have largely been left as bystanders, apart from sending air force protection to Saudi Arabia as it tries to fend off Houthi drone and missile assaults on its airports and energy installations.
The Middle Eastern states were represented by Fidan, Egypt’s Badr Abdelatty, Pakistan’s Ishaq Dar and Saudi Arabia’s Faisal bin Farhan. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia formed the Mecca defensive security pact in August, a grouping Egypt may join.
The European side was represented by Barrot, Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul and Italy’s Antonio Tajani. The agenda covered the Palestinian issue, including settlement expansion, settler violence and the two-state solution, as well as security in the strait of Hormuz, Yemen and efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war and prevent spillover into the Black Sea.
Wadephul said: “We are united by the impact these deadlocked conflicts are having on the economy and security of our countries and by the will to seek new ways to bring about solutions.”
He made no criticism of the US but accused “the Houthis and Iran of blackmailing world trade and continuing to stranglehold global supplies of energy and fertiliser”.
“We are feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping routes and whether at the petrol pump or the supermarket,” he said. “Elsewhere there is threat of famine.”
Tajani said the aim of the meeting was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.
“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he added. “If we want to reopen Hormuz, which is vital for our economies, we must promote dialogue and make Iran understand that this attitude cannot continue.”

items.title: Illegal Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs found inside state-owned China Telecom's network — Nvidia says chip smuggling is 'a drop in the bucket,' insists it remains a non-factor - Tom's Hardware
items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Lava, an Israeli security firm, says that it has been able to identify 32 Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 chips within the network of China Telecom, a state-owned company that provides telecommunications services within the country. These same chips have already been barred from export by U.S. export controls, a report by The Information notes, which begs the question of how they have turned up in a Chinese data center. Such chips can only be sold to whitelisted buyers who agree not to export them to sanctioned parties, including those in China.
However, banning companies from buying Nvidia's high-performance GPUs and AI data center chips hasn't always worked. In 2025, it was reported that Chinese companies smuggled $1 billion worth of Nvidia AI chips into the country in three months. At the time, the B200 chips were the most sought-after, but some distributors were already gearing up to sell B300-series chips when they became available.
While the latest finding shows that the proliferation of export-controlled chips into China continues to be an issue, Nvidia has downplayed the report but didn't deny the findings. "Governments, researchers, and media have all found insignificant diversion of controlled US products, less than one half of one percent in recent court cases — a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has," an Nvidia spokesperson told Tom's Hardware. "With tens of millions of GPUs in service in approved countries, this report again demonstrates that smuggling is a nonfactor, blocked by governments on both sides of the globe."
It's unknown how B300 chips found their way into China Telecom's server racks, nor can Lava confirm exactly where within the company's network they are located. But they are there, with Lava identifying them via Nvidia's own DCGM Exporter tool. The software can be installed by data center operators and is used to monitor server health and performance, and while designed for internal use, it can oftentimes be accessed beyond the data center's network. Oddly, it doesn't always require password authentication, either. Nvidia previously confirmed it was working on a tool that would allow its chips to be located , but it is yet to be released.
It's easy to see why Chinese firms are keen to get their hands on the Blackwell Ultra B300. Announced in March of last year , the data center GPU is one of the most powerful on the planet, offering huge performance gains with 50% more memory and FP4 compute than the previous-generation B200. At the time, Nvidia touted that the chip was "built for the age of reasoning," while name-checking more sophisticated AI LLMs like DeepSeek R1. At the time of its announcement, the B300 was expected to ship by the end of 2025, and it didn't take long for it to become hot property. In August 2026, nine people were indicted in Taiwan over the illegal export of B300 GPUs to China. This came just days after Supermicro confirmed that it had fired several employees following an investigation into smuggling. The complicated smuggling process included the use of a Taiwanese server trading firm called Flying Tiget Tech — a firm with whitelisted status for GPU purchases.
Nvidia's chips have proven so vital to AI data centers that demand for even its older silicon has caused skyrocketing prices. The company's A100 servers have tripled in price , despite being five years old, and can cost up to $82.,000. The ongoing crackdown on Nvidia chip smuggling has even seen some resort to retooling gaming GPUs to run AI workloads where possible.

items.title: If a Stock Market Crash Is on the Way, Warren Buffett Says This Is the Best Thing Investors Can Do for Their Portfolio - The Motley Fool
items.summary: If a Stock Market Crash Is on the Way, Warren Buffett Says This Is the Best Thing Investors Can Do for Their Portfolio  The Motley Fool
items.content:
The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -0.51% ) and Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -0.21% ) have recently been experiencing a bout of volatility after repeatedly notching record highs throughout 2026. With stocks coming under pressure, some investors are wondering whether a larger market correction is approaching.
Part of the concern stems from elevated bond yields and stubborn inflation. Meanwhile, artificial intelligence (AI) hyperscalers like Amazon , Microsoft , Alphabet , and Meta Platforms are among the companies supporting the broader economy as they accelerate spending on data centers .
Whether this volatility is just a temporary pullback or the beginning of something worse is impossible to know. But legendary investor Warren Buffett spent decades explaining how to navigate markets dominated by exciting new technologies, sky-high valuations, and uncertainty.
Former Berkshire Hathaway CEO Warren Buffett. Image source: Getty Images.
Revolutionary technology does not equal a good investment
Buffett built Berkshire Hathaway  into one of history's most successful investment firms simply because he had a relentless focus on businesses he understands. He generally avoided technology stocks, instead favoring industries such as insurance, banking, consumer products, utilities, and energy. These businesses usually have relatively predictable economics, which allowed Buffett to better assess their long-term earnings potential.
Buffett understood that an industry can revolutionize society without producing attractive returns overall. Consider the automobile and aviation industries as examples. Cars and airplanes have unquestionably transformed the global economy, but countless early manufacturers and airlines have gone bankrupt as competition intensified.
The theme here is that identifying which industries are game changers is much easier than choosing the specific companies that will capture profits in the long run. This distinction matters in today's AI environment.
While AI is shaping up to be one of the most transformative technologies in history, that doesn't mean every semiconductor company, software developer, or infrastructure provider is going to generate market-beating returns.
Is the AI revolution destined to end up like the dot-com bubble?
During the late 1990s, investors were pouring money into virtually anything that resembled the internet. Speculative technology stocks became multibaggers , even when the underlying companies had little revenue, no profits, or incomplete business models.
Reality inevitably caught up with expectations. After peaking in March 2000, the Nasdaq plummeted by 78% by October 2002. Suddenly, once-promising internet businesses left investors holding the bag.
Today, some investors are worried the AI boom could become a modern retelling of the dot-com bubble. Sure, AI leaders like Nvidia and the cloud hyperscalers already generate substantial profits and cash flow. The reason why is that their AI infrastructure is supported by numerous established businesses rather than simply promises around future growth. Still, the industry faces uncertainty because not every model developer is going to succeed in the long run.
This brings us to Buffett's most important investing principle. The single best thing an investor can do for their portfolio right now is load up on companies with durable competitive advantages rather than chasing the stocks attracting the most attention. Buffett describes these advantages as economic moats that come in the form of powerful brands, high switching costs, network effects , and economies of scale.
There's a more subtle lesson investors can learn from the dot-com crash: Time in the market is more valuable than trying to time the market. Suppose you invested in the S&P 500 near its peak during the dot-com era. If you managed to stay invested, you would have witnessed the index appreciate roughly 450%.
A hypothetical $10,000 investment would have grown to nearly $55,000, even though it was made right before a major market collapse. What's even more inspiring is that over the last 25 years, the S&P 500 has endured three recessions -- pictured above as the grey-shaded columns -- and managed to come out higher after each one. This underscores the resiliency of the S&P 500 as one of the greatest wealth-creation vehicles.
This performance is why Buffett's emphasis on diversification is both valuable and relevant in today's market. Rather than panic-selling whenever stocks become volatile or valuation is frothy, investors should rebalance their portfolios if their positions expose them to unnecessary risk.
Ultimately, no one knows whether the recent sell-off will permeate into a full-blown crash. But Buffett's philosophy offers a practical response: The best opportunity is to own quality businesses, avoid paying unreasonable prices, and remain patient enough to let compounding do the heavy lifting.

items.title: Are global oil reserves sufficient to withstand renewed US-Iran war? - Al Jazeera

Vessels are seen anchored off Bandar Abbas, Iran, along the Strait of Hormuz [File: Amirhossein Khorgooei/ISNA via AFP]
Oil prices have climbed towards their highest levels in five months as attacks on tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz mount and efforts to end the United States-Israel war on Iran are deadlocked.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose by more than $2 to $110.85 a barrel on Wednesday, close to a five-month peak.

A day earlier, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two tankers were “set ablaze” after hitting mines at what it called an illegal crossing point in the strait. Then, on Thursday, the IRGC said it hit seven more tankers although Washington dismissed the claim. In a statement, the IRGC said four of the vessels were transferring oil when they were targeted and caught fire overnight.
In September, the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized territory in Yemen close to the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical chokepoint into and out of the Red Sea and a gateway to Egypt’s Suez Canal.
The escalation came as the world’s emergency oil stocks, already tapped heavily since the Iran war began on February 28, sit at their lowest levels in decades.
Al Jazeera put a question to analysts: If fighting resumes in full, the Strait of Hormuz is shut off completely and Houthi attacks choke off Bab al-Mandeb, how long could the world’s reserves last?
Strategic oil reserves are stockpiles of crude oil and fuel held by governments or by companies on their behalf for use in a supply emergency.
The International Energy Agency (IEA), which was established in 1974 after the Arab oil embargo, coordinates most of them. Its importing members must hold at least 90 days of net imports. China and India are not members.
How much of the reserves has already been released this year?
On March 11, days after the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, the IEA’s 32 members agreed to make 400 million barrels available from emergency supplies, more than double the volume released after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The US pledged 172.2 million barrels from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) and Japan 79.8 million, according to IEA figures.
The SPR has since fallen to 283 million barrels, its lowest level since October 1982, according to the US Department of Energy.
Much of that oil was lent rather than sold and must be returned with extra barrels, according to the US Energy Information Administration.
Far less than before the war began in February, and not all of it can be used.
Aaron Kildow, a senior crude oil analyst at Sparta Commodities, told Al Jazeera that global strategic stocks excluding China and Iran have fallen by nearly 327 million barrels since the end of December 2025 with the US, Europe and Japan accounting for about 95 percent of the draw.
He estimated that leaves only about 400 million barrels of usable reserves worldwide, excluding China’s stockpile, which is unlikely to be exported, and Gulf stocks, which could be cut off by a total closure of Hormuz.
Nearly half of these available stocks are in Japan.
Europe has about 76 million barrels uncommitted, but members such as Germany are holding some back for a local emergency, Kildow said.
“Europe is the real wildcard, both on timing and willingness,” Kildow said.
Meanwhile, China’s onshore crude stocks stand at 1.13 billion barrels, down from 1.23 billion in late February but still enough for about 80 days of refinery intake, Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler, told Al Jazeera.
India’s reserves cover just eight days of its imports, the Reuters news agency reported.
What would a full closure of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb mean?
Before the war, about one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, or roughly 20 million barrels of oil a day, passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia has increased the amount of crude it transports from its oilfields in the east to its Red Sea port of Yanbu in the west via the East-West Pipeline, thereby bypassing Hormuz.
But there have been strikes on that pipeline, and tankers heading south from Yanbu must pass through Bab a-Mandeb, where the Iran-backed Houthis declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in July.
Only a confirmed 373,000 barrels a day of Saudi crude have transited Bab al-Mandeb so far this month, the lowest level since February, Xu said, with most Yanbu cargoes now heading north via Egypt instead.
If Hormuz were shut and the Houthis blocked all Saudi tankers, Gulf producers could export only through a few pipelines and Yanbu’s northbound route, Xu said.
That would leave about 7.5 million barrels a day of Middle Eastern crude, against 16.8 million now, a shortfall of about 9.3 million barrels a day, she estimated.
“If such attacks occur, the supply disruption could be even more severe and prolonged,” Xu said, referring to strikes on oilfields, terminals and pipelines.
Not for long – possibly just weeks, according to experts.
If Kpler’s estimated shortfall had to be covered entirely from the roughly 400 million usable barrels that Kildow identified, they could not, in practice, be released that fast. Japanese and South Korean reserves can move quickly, Kildow said, but US barrels are staged over three months, and Europe’s contribution is uncertain.
Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, said the world was fortunate after the first closure. “The salient feature of March and beyond was how a crisis didn’t actually develop. We got away with it,” he said.
“I don’t think the global economy will be as lucky next time if there is a protracted conflict,” Beauchamp said. “A month or two is all we have.”
The world would not literally run out of oil. Instead, prices would rise until enough demand disappeared. “One hundred fifty dollars [per barrel] becomes a very distinct possibility, which then sees significant demand destruction,” Beauchamp said.
The sharpest squeeze would be on diesel, which is already nearly double the price of crude, the IEA said.
Refiners would compete for crude grades rich in diesel, “a cost that ultimately lands on consumers,” Kildow said.
Most Gulf exports in September and October went to Asian buyers, and India and Pakistan are among the most exposed, Kildow said, adding that their nearest alternative supply, from West Africa, is 25 to 28 days away by sea, compared with two days from Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates.
“The squeeze won’t hit uniformly. It lands fastest and hardest where reserves are thinnest and substitute supply is farthest away,” Kildow said.
In the second quarter of this year, as the US-Iran war was under way, ExxonMobil reported earnings of $14.5bn, its highest in four years while Chevron posted $12bn, its best in six years and Shell more than doubled its earnings to nearly $10bn. Their profits are largely down to the high oil prices.
A second shock would send refiners scrambling for supplies from the US, Latin America, West Africa and Russia, Xu said.
“This would allow non-Middle Eastern producers to benefit from higher crude prices, potentially alongside lower transportation costs,” she said.

Oil price rises above $117 a barrel amid fears US will renew strikes on Iran
Brent crude increase follows Tehran threatening retaliatory attacks on Gulf refineries and datacentres
Oil has hit its highest level in more than six months as fears of fresh escalation in the Middle East conflict grip the energy markets.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose by about 3.5% on Friday to pass $117 a barrel at one point – its highest level since April.
The jump came after Tehran said it would attack oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities in the Gulf region if a new US-Israeli offensive was launched against Iran .
Richard Hunter, of the broker Interactive Investor, said: “Widespread reports that the US is considering renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections rather than pursuing a diplomatic route was enough for the price to pop, after what many had considered would be a brief conflict is now in its eighth month.”
The oil price later eased back slight to sit about 2.7% up at just over $116 a barrel. Brent crude had traded at about $72 a barrel back in February, before the Iran war began, but soared to touch $126 a barrel by the end of April.
Tensions in the region have been rising this week and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed to have struck four commercial ships in the strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. The US state department ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia , which has faced continued attacks from Houthi rebels in Yemen.
Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at the broker Wealth Club, said fears were rising that American and Israeli forces would be ordered to launch strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure after the US elections on 3 November.
She added: “At the same time, the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s facilities by Houthi rebels have intensified this week, and for ships attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz, it’s still a dangerous journey, with projectiles still being fired.”
Streeter said Ukraine’s bombardment of Russian diesel refineries was also adding to supply concerns.

Saudi Arabia wants to send 10 million barrels of oil a day around Hormuz. A former Treasury official says it may barely move prices
Saudi oil giant Aramco , officially the Saudi Arabian Oil Company, is racing to build a bigger back door around the Strait of Hormuz.
Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said this week that the company is working to raise the capacity of its East-West Crude Oil Pipeline, also known as the Petroline, to 10 million barrels a day from about 7 million today, while running engineering studies on additional export routes. Nasser made the comments to Al Arabiya Business in his first interview since the war began . The plan echoes an announcement earlier this month from Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, who told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh that the expansion would take two to three years .
The goal is to reduce the kingdom’s reliance on the Strait of Hormuz, which has been largely choked off since the U.S. and Israel launched a joint military attack on Iran on Feb. 28. Saudi crude production fell below 7 million barrels a day for much of the war’s first six months, down from more than 10 million before the conflict, and recovered to about 8 million in September, according to the International Energy Agency .
The Petroline spans Saudi Arabia, running roughly 750 miles from the Abqaiq processing hub near the Persian Gulf to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea . Before the war, it typically carried around 2 million barrels a day. Aramco ramped it up within weeks, and the line hit its full 7 million-barrel capacity by late March, with about 2 million of those barrels feeding Saudi refineries rather than export markets. The pipeline helped Aramco post a 25% jump in first-quarter profit . Adding another 3 million barrels a day would be a major undertaking.
But it may have little tangible impact on world fuel prices, according to Gilbert Metcalf , a visiting professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management and a former deputy assistant secretary for environment and energy at the U.S. Treasury Department.
“If—and this is a big if—the Saudis can increase pipeline flow to 10 million barrels per day, it will put about 2% more oil into the global marketplace,” Metcalf tells Fortune . “That could lower prices a bit, but there’s a lot of uncertainty here. The pipeline is vulnerable to drone and missile attacks, as is much of the Saudi petroleum infrastructure. And it’s not entirely clear that there is available refinery capacity to process the oil.”
That vulnerability isn’t hypothetical. The Petroline was first hit in May 2019, when Houthi drones struck a pumping station . This year it has been attacked repeatedly. An April 9 strike on a pumping station cut throughput by about 700,000 barrels a day before Saudi Arabia restored full capacity days later. On Sept. 10, drones struck the line in the Riyadh and Medina regions; Saudi officials said they were launched from Iraq . The attack forced a precautionary shutdown that lasted until Sept. 22, according to Kpler . And a Saudi energy-sector source told AFP that an Oct. 4 attack on a pumping station in Khurais halted flows again , though Bloomberg reported that oil continued to move.
The Red Sea end of the route is under pressure, too. Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia in July, have repeatedly attacked Saudi tankers, and in September seized control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab Strait , the southern gateway to the Red Sea. Southbound tankers leaving Yanbu must pass through it.
Even if the pipeline runs smoothly, a bigger Petroline might do little to ease the world’s dependence on Hormuz. “I don’t think moving more oil to the pipeline takes much pressure off opening the Strait of Hormuz,” Metcalf says. “Despite what the U.S. Treasury and Energy Departments are saying, it does not appear that oil is flowing through Hormuz at anywhere near levels observed before the U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran. Add to that threats in the Bab al-Mandab Strait and it’s clear that risks for Saudi oil production are as high now as they’ve ever been.”
Tanker data supports his skepticism. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said this month that Gulf crude flows had recovered to between 80% and 90% of prewar levels. But Kpler figures show oil exports through Hormuz averaged just under 9 million barrels a day in September , roughly 44% of February’s level. Gulf producers are pursuing longer-term workarounds as well: the UAE is fast-tracking a new pipeline of its own .
The Saudi government owns about 81.5% of Aramco. The kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund, the Public Investment Fund, holds 16%, and roughly 2.5% trades publicly . It is the world’s largest oil company and a major natural gas producer, with plans to raise gas output 80% by 2030 from 2021 levels. Yet even Aramco’s scale and an expanded pipeline may not be enough to shift the balance of power in the Middle East.
“The irony is that the balance of regional power has tilted from Saudi Arabia towards Iran as a result of the attacks on Iran,” Metcalf says. “This would have been unthinkable just a year ago.”

items.content:
In April, there was a major shift in the AI accelerator market, and for once, it didn’t come from Nvidia. Six months later, merchant TPUs are moving from announcement to commercial execution, with Google recognizing its first revenue from TPU systems in Q2 (from a small base). Last quarter, Cloud revenue growth accelerated to 82% for $24.8 billion, compared to $22.5 billion expected. In addition, new details around the TPU 8t show that Google’s threat to Nvidia is not limited to inference.
At the time, we pointed out that Google may be one of Nvidia’s strongest AI challengers , as Big Tech is closest to the problems that accelerators must solve. The problem that Google is prioritizing is lower cost per token, with token economics becoming a predominant concern as AI spending is pushing Big Tech’s free cash flows into the red.
Below, we discuss two reasons why Google’s AI story is about to change, not from advancements in AI software, but by going after one of the most profitable hardware businesses the tech industry has ever seen.
Two Financial Benefits to Custom Silicon and What TPU 8i Aims to Achieve
With Google reporting Q3 earnings next week, its TPU strategy could become a central focus of the earnings call, as merchant custom silicon addresses two major investor concerns. First, by lowering its cost per token, each dollar of capex stretches further. Secondly, selling TPUs to third-party customers creates an additional revenue stream for Google outside of monetizing capacity via cloud rentals.
Google’s newest TPU 8t and 8i both claim significant performance-per-dollar improvements over the prior generation, TPU v7 (Ironwood). This stems from increased HBM bandwidth , with 8t and 8i packing 216GB and 288GB respectively, up from Ironwood’s 192GB, as well as increased scale-up bandwidth, with 8i doubling Ironwood’s to 19.2 Tb/s.
With the TPU 8i, Google is addressing the problem of high costs (and consequently weak cash flows) through coherent shared memory, which plays a critical role in improving inference efficiency.
Arguably, the most critical point to understand about Google’s design advantage with the 8i is that the 331.8 TB of memory is shared across the entire pod over Google’s inter-chip interconnect (ICI). In our previous article, Google TPU v8 vs Nvidia: How Inference is Rewriting the AI Market we discussed that SRAM capacity and Boardfly topology also contribute to latency improvements.
Per our article, “Google noted that TPU 8i delivers up to an 80% performance-per-dollar improvement over the Ironwood TPU, particularly at low-latency targets for large MoE models.” This performance gain is not limited to 8i, as 8t offers up to 2.7X better performance-per-dollar on training.
To put this in different terms, this will allow customers to serve almost twice the volume at the same cost.
My updated Q4 Top 20 AI Stocks report hit inboxes this week. The report runs over 100 pages and identifies the 20 stocks I believe will lead the AI market this quarter. The report is built on the same investment discipline that drove our YTD outperformance and surfaced some of the biggest AI winners of 2026.
TPUs Help Gemini Deliver Competitive Cost per Intelligence Tasks
The benefit from this improved performance-per-dollar is evident in lower token costs, where Google offers among the lowest “cost per intelligence task.”
According to Artificial Analysis, cost per intelligence task reflects average prices for real-world evaluation scenarios, rather than just a simple per-million token price via APIs. In the evaluations, Gemini ranked among the lowest cost per intelligence compared to leading models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta.
For example, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview costs an average of $1.30, or 51% cheaper than GPT 5.5 (high) and 76% cheaper than Claude Sonnet 5.5. However, lightweight models such as GPT 6 Luna provide stiffer cost competition, with an average cost of $0.07 versus Gemini 3.8 Flash Lite’s $0.19.
Claude models rank as the most expensive to run, occupying the four highest-cost positions. Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview averages $1.30 per intelligence task versus $5.46 for Claude Sonnet 5.5 and $7.63 for Claude Fable 5.1. The 8i’s deployment would compound the already significant serving cost reductions Google achieved in 2025. Last Q4, Google’s CEO stated there was a 78% reduction in Gemini serving unit costs throughout 2025, with this occurring prior to the optimized v8 generation and the significant performance improvements it delivers.
As inference workloads shift from Ironwood to the new generation, that 80% reduction in performance-per-dollar can allow Google to continue lowering serving costs and help broaden Gemini adoption.
Third-Party TPU Sales Could Become Google’s Next Major Revenue Driver
Second, selling TPUs to third-party customers creates an additional revenue stream for Google outside of monetizing capacity via rentals. Google first made the shift to selling TPUs to third-party customers in April, recognizing the first TPU-related revenue in Q2 at a small scale.
Despite being quite early in this endeavor, its TPU customer list is notable. According to Broadcom’s update in Q3, Anthropic is deploying 1GW of Ironwood TPUs in 2026 , 5GWs of TPU 8i in 2027 and an incremental 10GW in 2028.
Meta signed a multibillion-dollar TPU deal in February and was rumored to explore third-party TPU deployments, while Google’s joint venture with Blackstone aims to bring its first 0.5 GW of TPU capacity online in 2027.
This rapid multi-GW ramp is expected to create a significant revenue stream for Google, with the majority of shipments starting to land in 2027 and beyond. Barclays projects third-party TPU sales could generate roughly $20 billion in revenue in 2026, more than triple to $67 billion in 2027 and more than triple again to $252.7 billion by 2028. This is one of the most aggressive ramps expected, with Piper Sandler and Morgan Stanley projecting just over $100 billion by 2028.
To put this in perspective, that 2028 projection from Barclays would imply that third-party TPU sales would ramp to the current run rate of Google’s Search business in just two and a half years.
Analysts project rapid growth in Google’s third-party TPU business through 2028. Barclays forecasts TPU sales reaching $252.7 billion by 2028, while Piper Sandler and Morgan Stanley estimate approximately $104 billion and $108 billion, respectively. However, this secondary revenue stream currently comes with a fair degree of risk. At the moment, Anthropic accounts for the majority of expected third-party shipments, creating customer concentration and financing risk for TPU shipments.
Merchant TPU Sales Shift the Capex Burden to Customers
This secondary revenue stream from selling TPUs also shifts the capex burden away from Google to its third-party customers. With $200 billion earmarked towards capex this year, any incremental revenue that doesn’t require Google to build the data center first is unusually valuable.
For Google to deploy TPUs through Google Cloud and rent them to customers, it must first pay upfront for the data center, the power, the cooling and the chips, reflected in its 2026 capex bill at $195-205 billion. Once TPUs are installed and energized, Google can then recover its capex by renting these chips out in the cloud across several years.
However, merchant TPU sales to third-party customers flip that equation around. Under this sales model, customers would fund the data center and the hardware purchases, with Google’s revenue coming at chip delivery instead of those multi-year rental terms. Thus, that estimated $253 billion revenue stream would appear in financials as systems are shipped.
One major drawback to shifting capex to its customers is that R&D labs such as Anthropic, who accounts for the majority of projected shipments, do not enjoy the same balance sheet strength as hyperscalers. While Anthropic says it was cash flow positive in Q3, it does not have the same strength in terms of cash as the hyperscalers do. If Google plays a larger role in helping finance chip purchases (where Broadcom currently is active with its AI XPV platform), some of the cash benefit shifts back onto Google’s balance sheet or into contingent obligations.

One caveat to external TPU revenue is that it could weigh on Google’s margins, as TPU system sales will carry a far lower margin than cloud revenue.
For context, Google Cloud reported an operating margin of 35.6% as of Q2, expanding roughly 15 points YoY as operating income more than tripled to $8.8 billion as AI services ramped.
However, by shifting to selling full TPU racks, revenue will now include HBM, networking components, cooling and power, much of which will pass through at little markup. Broadcom offers a clear example for this, noting that as “TPUs continue to accelerate, there’ll be pressure overall on margins” as these lower-margin systems contribute a higher proportion of AI semiconductor revenue.

The report is built on the same investment discipline that drove our YTD outperformance and surfaced some of the biggest AI winners of 2026.
For Google, margin impacts could be more pronounced, as it’s expected that third-party TPU sales will carry far lower margins than even what Broadcom realizes. Even with the higher mix of lower-margin XPU projects, Broadcom is maintaining a mid-70% gross margin, though Morgan Stanley estimates that Google’s third-party TPU sales could carry a gross margin of just 30%.
Impacts in the near-term are likely to be relatively minimal as TPU revenue should be easily absorbed by its broader cloud suite, but come later in 2027 and especially 2028, the higher mix of TPU-driven revenue (potentially outpacing broader Cloud services) could weigh on segment margins.
Google’s Challenge to Nvidia Extends Beyond Inference
While the 8i targets inference workloads, new details on the training-focused TPU 8t show how far Google is pushing scale.
At Hot Chips in August, Google outlined an 8t ‘superpod’ of 9,600 chips with access to 2PB of shared HBM and 121 exaflops of FP4 compute, offering roughly twice the performance-per-watt of Ironwood. The scale is made possible by Google’s optical circuit switches, which can dynamically carve slices out of a 9,600-chip pod. Compare this to Nvidia’s current rack-scale systems, where the scale-up domain tops out at 72 GPUs.
Google is also taking this scale a step further with the introduction of its dedicated Virgo Network fabric. With Virgo, Google can link together fourteen of the ‘superpods’ in a single fabric, capable of supporting 134,400 TPUs in a single domain with 47 PB/s of bandwidth. This cluster size offers 1.6 yottaflops of compute (or 1.6 million exaflops) for massive, large-scale frontier model training.
According to AMD at CES 2026, “Reaching yottascale AI compute would require the equivalent of millions of today’s Frontier exaflop-class supercomputers operating together.”
Nvidia Delay Could Help Google; But it’s Not Necessary
As we’ve said in the past, Nvidia’s product roadmap has consistently pushed the limits across the supply chain. This led to a delay in 2024 on Blackwell, due to the systems overheating.
In May, we discussed a reported one-quarter delay in Nvidia’s Rubin ramp, stating:
“Lastly, the reported one-quarter delay of Nvidia’s Rubin ramp, officially scheduled for Q3 2026, could offer a strong argument for diversification across AI accelerators. Notably, TrendForce revised its estimate of Rubin’s contribution to Nvidia’s total high-end GPU shipments for 2026 down from 29% to 22% to account for such a delay.
Factors contributing to the reported delay and TrendForce’s revision include “the time required to validate the newer HBM4 memory used by the chips, challenges with the migration to Nvidia’s faster ConnectX-9 NICs, the system’s higher overall power consumption, and the more advanced liquid cooling requirements.”
Since then, another report has surfaced. In July, CNBC reported that SemiAnalysis found Nvidia’s Kyber rack architecture had been delayed by more than 12 months to 2028, citing a PCB midplane manufacturing issue, though Nvidia has publicly disputed the report.
If these reports prove accurate on the Kyber rack delay, or even if Nvidia shifts the Rubin Ultra architecture from its original planned four-die design to a “2+2” design as rumored, the impacts would be larger than just timing. Kyber marks the system that expands Nvidia’s scale-up domain from 72 GPUs to 576 GPU dies per rack.
A delay to 2028 would mean Nvidia’s largest coherent domain stays in the 72-GPU class through 2027, the same year Google’s merchant TPU revenue is set to ramp with pods of 1,152 chips for inference and 9,600 chips for training (slightly larger than the 9,216-chip pod with Ironwood).
Google is also quickly catching up to Nvidia in terms of unit volume, although a majority of these will be used internally to serve Gemini. However, any potential delay on Nvidia’s roadmap could open the door for further market share gains, as estimated TPU volumes range from 8.8 to 10 million in 2027, above UBS’ estimate for 8.8 million Rubin chips next year.
HBM Supply Constraints Remain the Largest Bottleneck
HBM is the leading constraint the AI industry faces, and commentary from industry executives suggests that the shortage is only worsening with little relief expected in 2027 or even 2028.
In our recent newsletter, Why Nvidia’s SK Hynix Deal Leaves Little AI Memory Supply , we explained that based on industry estimates, Nvidia and Alphabet are expected to demand roughly three-quarters of global HBM supply in 2027. When factoring in AMD’s Helios ramp and numerous custom silicon projects at other hyperscalers, there is little chance for meaningful HBM supply relief or allocation increase.
Faced with such tight supply constraints, even Nvidia, the largest buyer, is paying up to secure access to HBM, and Google likely is having to do the same given its allocation is nearly on par with Nvidia’s, and far ahead of AMD’s.
With the memory market recently shifting in favor of long-term agreements with substantial prepayments, it means cash goes out the door long before TPU revenue is recognized. Customer deposits for third-party TPU capacity can offset this, but it’s a timing drag during a ramp, which is exactly what 2027 will be.
Google’s greatest competitive advantage may not be building a faster chip than Nvidia, but rather in building AI infrastructure at a lower cost. The company has spent years designing accelerators around the demands of its own AI workloads, giving it an advantage that traditional chip companies cannot easily replace.
Selling TPUs to third-party customers opens up a new revenue stream for Google, with analysts forecasting a wide range of revenue from $100 billion to $250 billion as soon as 2028. The higher-end of those forecasts represents what took Search decades to achieve.
The one caveat? HBM constraints and customer financing could limit how quickly the sales translate to improved cash flow. Read more here .

Detroit, Michigan – The first question in the United States Senate debate in Michigan between Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed and his Republican rival Mike Rogers was about the issue that appears to matter most to voters – the economy.
El-Sayed quickly drew a contrast between himself and Rogers, who is backed by US President Donald Trump. It was not about interest rates, taxes, or trade policy. It was about the US-Israel war on Iran .

“Right now, the cost of gas, the cost of groceries, it all really goes back to this war in Iran,” the progressive Democrat said on Wednesday.
“We need a War Powers Resolution rather than a senator who wants to stand hip-to-hip with Donald Trump on this war that made no sense when it started and certainly makes no sense now.”
El-Sayed was referring to legislative efforts to curb Trump’s ability to continue the eight-month conflict .
Across Michigan, Democrats are emphasising their opposition to the war to woo voters stung by rising gas and grocery prices.
“The war in Iran is a kitchen table issue,” said Jonathan Guyer, programme director at the Institute for Global Affairs (IGA).
“Voters don’t often rank foreign policy as their top issue, but I think it’s so interwoven with the economy right now that essentially foreign policy is the economy.”
IGA released a survey last month suggesting that 60 percent of potential voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of the war. More alarmingly for Republicans, an overwhelming majority of respondents – 81 percent – agreed that the conflict has raised the cost of living.
Almost immediately after Israel and the US started attacking Iran on February 28, Tehran began disrupting the flow of energy products through the Strait of Hormuz – sending oil and gas prices skyrocketing.
In the US, the price of diesel – which is used to power heavy machinery, including heavy trucks that ship consumer goods across the country – has reached record highs over the past weeks.
Likewise, petrol or gasoline has become less affordable. Average Americans feel that uptick firsthand almost daily at the gas pump.
The average price of one gallon (3.8 litres) of petrol has gone from less than $3 before the war to more than $4.27 as of Thursday, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).
The increased cost of energy and transportation has trickled down to the entire economy, fuelling inflation at a time when affordability had become one of the key issues in US electoral politics.
Trump and his allies have argued that the war was necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
But before the war, Trump himself had said repeatedly that Iran’s nuclear programme had been “obliterated” by the June 2025 US strikes against the country’s uranium enrichment facilities.
And US intelligence officials have testified to Congress that they have no evidence that Iran is building a nuclear bomb.
Rogers, the Michigan Senate candidate, pushed to defend the war during the debate on Wednesday.
“You want to pay $8 [for] a gallon of gas, let Iran get a nuclear weapon. You lose control of that whole region,” he said.
At the same time, Rogers has also called for an end to the conflict.
In a recent campaign commercial filmed in a grocery store , the Republican candidate said, “The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly.”
The position is echoed by other Republicans in tough House and Senate races.
In neighbouring Ohio, Senator Jon Husted has called for a “quick” end to the war as well. In Iowa, Congresswoman Ashley Hinson, who is running for the Senate, said she told Trump that the conflict should come to an “immediate and successful end”. In Maine, Senator Susan Collins has highlighted her vote in favour of several War Powers Resolutions.
Still, Trump, who is the leader of the Republican Party, has suggested that he may renew all-out fighting with Iran after the midterm vote next month, and he has promoted the war as a historic success.
“I think it’s one of the greatest things we’ve done. We’ve stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon,” Trump told reporters on Wednesday.
“It’s one of the best things that we’ve done, and it took a lot of courage to do it because no other president was willing to do it.”
Despite the overall unpopularity of the war, most Republicans continue to support it.
A Pew Research Center poll released earlier this month showed that 63 percent of Republican respondents said they approve of Trump’s handling of the conflict.
The IGA survey, taken in August, put the number at 74 percent. But only 24 percent of Republican respondents said they “strongly approve” of Trump’s handling of the war – down from 40 percent in April.
Guyer suggested that the lack of enthusiastic support for the war in the Republican base may hurt the party in the upcoming elections.
“It means that Republicans aren’t necessarily walking away from the president, but their support for him has a lot less conviction,” he told Al Jazeera.
“That could have implications if they actually show up to vote [and] if they are going to be involved in campaigning.”
With the elections less than two weeks away, it’s apparent that the Democrats see the war as an Achilles heel for Republicans, and they are invoking the conflict incessantly to undermine Trump-backed candidates all over the country.
Democratic Senator Chris Murphy addresses Abdul El-Sayed supporters at a debate watch party in Dearborn, Michigan, the US, October 21 [Ali Harb/Al Jazeera] At a Senate debate watch party attended by dozens of El-Sayed’s supporters in Detroit on Wednesday, Al Jazeera asked Democratic Senator Chris Murphy – who recently returned from a visit to the Middle East – about the war. His answer was all about the US economy, not the geopolitics of the region.
“Well, diesel prices here in Detroit are already above $6 a gallon, and they’re going to go higher if this war restarts. Mike Rogers just said in the debate that he’s going to support the war, which is basically a death sentence for the American economy,” Murphy told Al Jazeera.
“There’s a big choice for Michigan voters to make here. If you want this war to continue for another year, if you want gas prices to climb to $8 a gallon, vote for Mike Rogers. If you want the war to end, if you want prices to come down, then vote for Abdul El-Sayed .”

items.title: White House says the US is lifting tariffs on some Canadian goods
items.summary: Susan Collins, a Republican in a tight race to keep her senate seat in next month's elections, said she had been working with the White House on tariff relief.
items.content:
Image caption, Senator Susan Collins said she had worked with the administration to secure "tariff relief"
The US is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods, with the White House saying on Friday it was working to "protect the economic prosperity and national security of the American people".
The exemptions could also boost Republican candidates in the midterms elections on 3 November, as many US voters list affordability and economic pressures as top issues.
Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race in Maine to keep her seat in the election, first announced the exemptions, saying they would help her state's agriculture industry.
After trade talks collapsed this summer, the US and Canada started an escalating tariff war that has affected both sides of the border.
The White House, in a statement, said the US was removing certain products from the list of Canadian goods it taxes, such as plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and certain packing crates and boxes.
It added those items would be replaced with certain valves, carpets, waste products, among others.
The BBC has contacted the White House, US commerce department and trade representative for further comment.
Also on Friday, President Donald Trump said that Canada is "working very hard" on a â trade âdeal with the US.
The Wall Street Journal reported that the exemptions, largely focused on Canadian agricultural and forestry, were made in a bid to help Collins and other Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections.
The reductions could be offset by raising levies on âother Canadian goods, the Journal reported.
In a statement Collins issued shortly after the report, the incumbent lawmaker, who is trying to clinch her sixth term, said that nine categories of products, including blueberry, potato, apple, and âseaweed producers, will be exempted from US tariffs on Canada.
"Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense," she said on X.
Collins said she has asked US officials and senior administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada.
âMaine's economy, as well as that of other border states, is deeply linked to Canada and have felt the effects of the month-long trade war.
Michigan lawmaker Mike Rogers, also a Republican, has aired adverts calling on Trump to end the standoff in his trade-reliant state after spending months supporting the policy,
In New Hampshire, former Senator John Sununu has also been critical of the retaliatory tariffs.

items.title: The Iran war’s toxic impact on one of the planet’s most unique seas - CNN
items.summary: The Iran war’s toxic impact on one of the planet’s most unique seas  CNN
items.content:
The conflict in the Middle East is shaping up to be yet another US war with a toxic legacy .
Bombs and missiles have released heavy metals and harmful chemicals into the atmosphere. US-Israeli and Iranian strikes have hit oil facilities, igniting fires that covered Tehran in thick black smoke and oil-saturated rain , exposing millions to pollution which could have long-lasting health impacts.
And these strikes are also affecting the Persian Gulf. Attacks on ships and oil infrastructure in the waterway have produced oil spills visible from space .
A spill from a tanker has temporarily closed beaches in the Emirate of Umm Al Quwain with authorities working to contain the environmental impacts, according to an announcement Thursday by the United Arab Emirates Ministry of Climate Change and Environment.
It’s not been confirmed whether the spill is linked to Iranian attacks but it’s yet another sign of the huge risks faced by the Persian Gulf, one of the world’s most delicate and unique marine systems.
As the conflict continues, experts are warning of a broader contamination crisis.
Go beyond the forecast with stunning stories and visuals.
For months, cargo ships and oil tankers have been targeted in the Strait of Hormuz, the vital shipping route for oil and gas between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman.
The progression from vessel impact to environmental damage is clear to see in many cases, said Brian Barnes, who is part of a group of satellite oceanographers at the University of South Florida analyzing the effects of this war from afar.
“Some of the major ships that have been targeted, we see prolonged plumes, stretching for hundreds of kilometers away from the impact site,” Barnes said.
The Persian Gulf has long suffered from oil pollution, but research by Barnes and other scientists comparing March 2026, when fighting was intense, with the same period last year shows a sharp increase.
An oil tanker burns after being hit by an Iranian strike in the ship-to-ship transfer zone at Khor al-Zubair port near Basra, Iraq, March 11, 2026.
“What we’re seeing is twice the amount of surface oil in the Persian Gulf area relative to what we would expect in the absence of a major conflict,” Barnes said.
Although, he noted, satellite imagery can only show what is on the surface of the water and not the thickness of the oil, which would give a more accurate picture of the extent of the contamination.
What is harder to assess with limited physical access to the conflict-riddled waterway is the impact on marine wildlife.
The Persian Gulf hosts an ecosystem teeming with life. It is home to several species of sea turtles, hundreds of species of fish and the world’s second-largest population of dugongs, or sea cows.
“One of the world’s largest whale shark congregations occurs close to the South Pars oil field where Qatar and Iran meet,” said Bernhard Riegl, a professor at Nova Southeastern University who has studied the Persian Gulf for decades.
Sandy offshore islands and expansive seagrass beds make the Gulf an ideal habitat for nesting and breeding. Extensive mangrove forests and coral reef structures create protected nurseries for dolphins, seabirds, and whale sharks. Yet in springtime, traditionally the season for breeding, the war was raging.
A view of the vibrant underwater world at one of Musandam's popular diving sites in Khasab, Oman on August 28, 2025.
A satellite image shows oil in the Persian Gulf on April 2, 2026.
Only the hardiest marine life survives in these waters. Not only is the Persian Gulf one of the world’s hottest seas, but it also experiences sharp temperature changes throughout the year.
The water near Kuwait City, for example, goes from highs of around 36 degrees Celsius (97 Fahrenheit) in the height of summer to lows of around 16 degrees Celsius (60 Fahrenheit).
Razan Khalifa Al Mubarak, the UAE’s special envoy of the Minister of Foreign Affairs for Nature, called for an end to attacks on the Gulf in an editorial earlier this year.
“While the financial costs of damage can be calculated, the loss of ecosystems and species cannot. Once degraded, these systems may not recover,” she wrote.
The forecast is just the beginning. We’ll send you expert coverage and the stories behind the weather — so you always know more than just the number. Sign up for the newsletter
Contamination in the Gulf brings unique challenges as the body of water is relatively shallow — the deepest areas are only around 360 feet — and it is small, at 93,000 square miles. It also has only one entry and exit point connecting it to the open ocean: the Strait of Hormuz, which leads into the Gulf of Oman and the Indian Ocean beyond. This all means pollutants tend not to disperse or dilute easily.
No matter which country or vessel may be a target during this war, the repercussions will have wide impacts, Riegl said: “If we take a drop of oil and put it into the water on the Iranian side of the inflow into the Gulf, a year later it will be in Kuwait, two years later it will be on the Omani side of the Gulf and float out there.”
The 1991 Gulf War should be a cautionary tale, Riegl said. Retreating Iraqi forces set fire to hundreds of oil wells in Kuwait creating an environmental catastrophe felt throughout the Gulf.
An oil well fire at the Greater Burhan oil field in Kuwait, in August 9, 1991.
“The shorelines were devastatingly affected,” Riegl said. “In fact, in many areas of Saudi (Arabia), if you go and dig in the sand, there’s still old oil in there. It’s just very hard to get rid of.”
An additional concern is the fact that tens of millions of Gulf residents rely on desalination plants, which convert seawater into drinking water.
The six countries which form the Gulf Cooperation Council produce around a third of the world’s desalinated water. Bahrain and Kuwait are almost entirely dependent on desalination for all drinking water. Oil pollution in the Gulf could damage these facilities, imperiling water supply .
When hundreds of millions of gallons were intentionally released into the Persian Gulf during the Iraq war, Kuwait had to rely on Saudi Arabia, Turkey and others to provide hundreds of water tankers and trucks to deliver bottled water.
One perhaps unexpected repercussion of environmental damage in the Persian Gulf is that it could undermine scientists’ understanding of the impacts climate change will have on the world’s seas.
The Gulf’s high temperatures are roughly where marine tropics are expected to be around the year 2100, Riegl said.
A flock of birds near the shores of the Daymaniyat Islands Nature Reserve in Oman, on October 4, 2023.
The Gulf has “some of the most… valuable genetics of any sea on Earth, because a lot of the adaptation that will need to be done has already been achieved in the Gulf.”
“If we want to know what the ocean at large will look like at the end of the century,”he added, “the Gulf is the area to look at.”
CNN’s Kim Kelaita and Hiba Khurram contributed reporting.

items.title: FCC issues first bans under new chip-level rule — dashcam and video transmitter carried Huawei AI silicon with face tracking - Tom's Hardware
items.summary: The FCC recently imposed a new rule allowing it to ban devices based on the internal chips instead of basing bans on individual products or brands, thus closing the loophole of rebranded products with parts from Chinese manufacturers on US export restriction lists. Using this new rule, the FCC has banned two devices from being sold and marketed in the US for the first time: a dashboard camera and
items.content:
The FCC recently imposed a new rule allowing it to ban devices based on the internal chips instead of basing bans on individual products or brands, thus closing the loophole of rebranded products with parts from Chinese manufacturers on US export restriction lists. Using this new rule, the FCC has banned two devices from being sold and marketed in the US for the first time: a dashboard camera and a wireless video transmitter. As reported by The Verge, these devices were banned due to the HiSilicon Smart Vision SoC (System on a Chip) they contain, which features built-in detection algorithms for faces. HiSilicon is a subsidiary of Huawei, and the firm and its subsidiaries are on the FCC's Covered List of entities that pose a risk to US national security .
The Hi3516CV610 UHD Smart Vision is an SoC for surveillance and camera products. The SoC is meant to be used for things like vehicle dashcams and wireless CCTV systems; fully equipped with WiFi, Ethernet, video encoding chips, an Arm Cortex-A7, and an NPU (Neural Processing Unit) for AI features. The NPU is what the FCC is concerned about, explaining that it is a device that contains logic-bearing "smart" components produced by entities on the Covered List.
(Image credit: HiSilicon) On the SoC's data sheet, the Intelligent Video Engine (IVE) uses the NPU that runs a built-in dedicated multimodal large model and transformer feature acceleration. The transformer feature acceleration allows the AI model to understand the relationship between objects from one video frame to another, keeping "attention" between related objects: pets, faces, human figures, and parcels, as the data sheet advertises. For consumers, this potentially means the AI in a surveillance camera can understand whether it is your pet that is escaping, or an unknown person is stealing your parcel after understanding that it was placed by a courier worker.
However, the FCC believes the logic-bearing AI in the SoC can do something much more nefarious, surveying US citizens and logging faces for foreign surveillance. Huawei already had a previous AI chip scandal , using shell companies to deceive TSMC into producing AI chips for them, going against the US' request for TSMC to halt supplies to a list of Chinese customers; among other Huawei scandals leading to other product bans in the US.

items.title: Oil spill washes up on UAE beaches after tanker strike
items.summary: Satellite images show oil spreading for miles along the coastline, threatening local marine wildlife
items.content:
By Thomas Copeland, Mark Poynting and Tom Spencer BBC Verify
An oil spill from a tanker attacked near the Strait of Hormuz is spreading along the United Arab Emirates (UAE) coastline, forcing the closure of some beaches and coastal areas.
Satellite images from Monday show the beginnings of the oil spill from a ship matching the location and dimensions of Gem No.2, which was damaged between 9 and 10 October during a record surge of vessel strikes by Iran .
The slick of oil had spread more than 35km (22 miles) from the tanker by Wednesday, the satellite imagery showed.
UAE authorities said on Thursday that the incident is affecting beaches near the northern city of Umm Al Quwain and verified video from Friday shows the oil washing ashore, colouring the water black.
The UAE's Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Thursday that it "immediately began containment" in order to "limit environmental impacts".
Prof Steve Widdicombe, director of Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre in the UAE, told BBC Verify it was "inevitable that there will be an impact", but researchers caution it is too soon to assess extent of the damage.
Initially a much smaller oil leak could be seen emerging from the ship on 19 October.
But the slick appears to have rapidly spread over two days, according to radar satellite imagery reviewed by BBC Verify and intelligence firm MAIAR.
Oil spills can cause immediate deaths of marine animals and other organisms, for example by physically trapping turtles, smothering the feathers of seabirds or damaging the gills of fish.
They can also cause longer-lasting damage, Prof Widdicombe said, if species remain exposed to toxic compounds from the oil which could impact their ability to reproduce.
Researchers have cautioned the environmental impact at this stage is very uncertain, as it depends on factors including the volume and type of oil spilled, how quickly it evaporates or breaks down and the effectiveness of the clean-up operation.
But the spill does extend towards Siniyah and Khor Al Beidah islands, a globally recognised Key Biodiversity Area containing habitats like corals, seagrasses and saltmarshes, as well as species including green turtles and the critically endangered Halavi guitarfish.
The proximity of the spill to this area is the "most concerning environmental angle", according to Eoghan Darbyshire, a scientist at the Conflict and Environment Observatory.
BBC Verify analysis of the dimensions and location of the ship indicate they match a crude oil tanker called Gem No.2.
Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard reported the Panama-flagged tanker was "struck by an unknown projectile" on 9 October, just north of the town of Al Jazeera Al Hamra, causing a fire on board that was later extinguished.
Verified footage first posted on social media on 10 October showed the crew running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rose over the ship.
Iranian state media shared footage of a ship matching Gem No.2 which appeared to show the vessel on fire with burning oil spilling into the sea.
The ship had been attempting to exit the Strait of Hormuz via an "unauthorized and dangerous route", according to state media.
All 22 Indian crew members were rescued, the Indian consulate in Dubai said on 11 October.
Gem No.2 is one of a record number of ships that reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz at the start of October .
Security experts told BBC Verify this was part of an Iranian effort to assert greater control over the strait, in response to the US military successfully escorting more vessels through the vital shipping lane.
Tankers and other commercial vessels have come under attack from both Iranian and US forces in and around the Strait of Hormuz amid the conflict between the two countries.
Another major oil slick washed up on the shores of Iran's Qeshm Island in August , which experts said threatened wildlife, protected ecosystems and fishing communities.

items.title: Defense giant Saab sees orders triple after Gripen fighter jet deal with Ukraine
items.summary: European governments race to turn defense spending pledges into military capability, boosting companies' order books.
items.content:
Saab Q3 earnings: Fighter jet maker beats expectations as orders triple
Swedish defense giant Saab on Friday reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and sales, while orders trippled.
New orders came in at 65.8 billion Swedish kronor, up from 20.9 billion kronor a year earlier.
"The growing customer demand is reflected in major contract awards, including Gripen for Ukraine, GlobalEye and an order related to Germany's new frigates," CEO Micael Johansson said.
Swedish defense giant Saab reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and revenue on Friday, as new orders more than tripled from a year earlier, boosted by a deal to supply Gripen fighter jets to Ukraine.
New orders came in at 65.8 billion Swedish kronor ($6.6 billion), up from 20.9 billion kronor a year earlier, beating FactSet expectations of 56.4 billion kronor.
Third-quarter sales reached 20.6 billion kronor, ahead of FactSet expectations of 20 billion kronor. Earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) came in at 1.95 billion kronor, also beating forecasts of 1.9 billion kronor.
Stockholm-listed shares closed 1.8% higher Friday, amid a mixed defense sector. The Stoxx 600 index ended the session down 0.3%.
The results come as European governments race to turn defense spending pledges into military capability.
Saab's order intake included a 24.6 billion kronor contract for 16 Gripen E fighter jets with the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration for Ukraine, signed in June and booked in the third quarter. Deliveries are scheduled for 2029-2030.
"The growing customer demand is reflected in major contract awards, including Gripen for Ukraine, GlobalEye and an order related to Germany's new frigates," CEO Micael Johansson said in a statement.
Orders booked in the quarter also include a 10.1 billion kronor order for its military surveillance aircraft GlobalEye to an undisclosed customer in the Middle East, and an 8.7 billion kronor order to equip warships for the German Navy.
Saab, whose products range from Gripen fighter jets and submarines to missiles and advanced electronics, has seen exponential order growth since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
Even with an ever-growing order book , booming sales, and increasing profitability, Saab stock, like many of its peers, has taken a hit in recent months as some investors question whether valuations have run ahead of the industry's ability to deliver.
Rising geopolitical tensions, including recent airspace violations, drone incidents and ongoing conflicts, are driving demand for defense capabilities, Johansson said. He added that Saab is expanding production capacity and investments to help it meet growing customer needs.
"The long-term market outlook remains favourable," he said, as Saab reported that the order growth was driven by a more than sixfold surge in large orders to 52.1 billion kronor, while small orders rose 84% and medium-sized orders fell 16%.
The total order backlog amounted to 364.2 billion at the end of September, up from 274.5 billion at the beginning of the year, marking a sixth consecutive quarter of order book growth.
Saab CEO: Europe needs joint defense procurement and industry partnerships
In July, Saab said it was looking to boost its production of jets from 15 per year to between 20 and 30.
"We can go further than that if we now get sort of partners involved in a more substantial way," Johansson told CNBC at the time.
Johansson also emphasized that European governments must fundamentally rethink how they buy weapons, moving away from fragmented national procurement toward long-term partnerships with industry.
